messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Known People: Related people, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rafiq Khan was 49 years old, married, and worked as a military medic, a role that had long depended on his calm under pressure and his ability to move quickly toward other people’s injuries rather than away from them. He was referred for help after months of feeling increasingly unable to function with the same steadiness he once brought to work and home. The event he described as the beginning of all this had happened in a relationship that, from the outside, had not fit the image of danger he now carried with him. He had been physically abused by a romantic partner, and what still stood out most clearly to him was not one single blow but the repeated sense of being trapped in close quarters with someone whose anger he could not predict. He spoke about the assault in fragments, struggling to turn it into a linear story, as if the details would not stay in language long enough to be told. At points he simply gestured to his ribs and shoulders and said that when he tried to remember it, he felt it again there.

In the months after the abuse ended, Rafiq noticed that the memories did not come to him as ordinary recollections. When they returned, they arrived with the force of something immediate, as if the frightening event were happening right now rather than years ago. He said that at those moments his body reacted before he could think, and the same parts of him that had been hurt then would ache now, with a physical pain he experienced as unmistakably linked to the event. He could not easily describe the episode in words, even when he tried to explain it to his wife, because the memory seemed to bypass language and settle in his body first. He had begun to avoid wearing clothes that reminded him of that period, especially similar clothes that had been associated with the time of the abuse, choosing different outfits with unusual care. He also stopped exercising, even though physical conditioning had once been part of his routine as a medic, because exertion left him feeling too exposed in his own body and too close to sensations he did not want to notice. Over time, he also started avoiding other people more generally, turning down invitations and keeping interactions brief, as if distance from others might reduce the chance of being cornered, questioned, or made to feel known in ways that could become dangerous.

His daily life became organized around what felt safe in only a very limited number of places. He could relax briefly at home in a few specific rooms, but even there he stayed watchful. Falling asleep had become difficult because he felt he needed to stay alert, and he lay awake listening for signs that something was wrong. Ordinary sounds startled him more than they used to, and he would jump at noises that most people would barely notice. At work, the hospital and base environments that once felt familiar became harder to tolerate when they brought him into contact with police officers, known people related to the situation, or even with men whose sweat or body odour unexpectedly carried him back to the old threat. A police presence in particular could make him tense immediately, not because he had done anything wrong, but because the sight of authority nearby seemed to tighten all the old feelings of being trapped and exposed. He became more guarded around anyone connected to the people involved in the abuse, and he was uneasy when he encountered body odour or sweat in crowded practical spaces such as locker rooms or treatment areas, where the smell could seem to pull him back with sudden vividness.

As the months passed, Rafiq found himself questioning his own worth in painful ways. He had come to believe that there was something wrong with him as a person, not because anyone had said it directly, but because he could not understand how he had ended up in a situation where he was hurt and still felt so altered afterward. He also felt deeply that the people responsible had faced no consequences, and that sense of unfinished accountability left him angry and hollow at the same time. He said that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, a statement that seemed to come from a man who had once anchored himself in service, competence, and responsibility, but now found those roles harder to inhabit with conviction. What finally brought him to seek help was the growing pressure of these experiences in both his marriage and his work: his wife was worried about how much he kept to himself, and he no longer trusted himself to simply push through at night or in the unpredictable environments of military medicine. He came hoping for some way to sleep without scanning for danger, to move through more than a handful of places without fear, and to understand whether he could ever feel like himself again.
